attributes.title: Level 5

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Notice there is already code in the editor; there are image variables under the comment // image set up. 


Underneath this starter code, add comments with these descriptions to the project: game set up, function set up, game events. Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you define a new function with 3 number parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the spawnFlame function is called?

❓ What type of parameters should the spawnFlame function’s 3 parameters be set to?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Functions can be useful for defining a chunk of code that can be easily reused throughout a project. They also help organize the code in the editor by creating simple function calls within a chunk of code. 

💡 Point out to the ninja that just as when creating an empty array, when adding parameters to a function, the type must be defined. In this example, the spawnFlame function should be defined with 3 number parameters.
steps.instructions:
Create a function with 3 parameters to create moving Enemy sprites!


Click Advanced then open Functions and drag [function doSomething] underneath // function set up. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

function doSomething() {...} 

Rename the function spawnFlame then add 3 number parameters that will set the sprite’s x-position, y-position, and image scale. Inside the function’s parentheses, type the parameter names (x, y, and scale) and a colon :, then set the type to number. Add a comma between each parameter.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use /** to write a comment that will appear in the documentation box whenever the cursor hovers over the spawnFlame function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is using /** to write a comment different from how comments have previously been added to the JavaScript editor?

❓ Why might it be useful to document a custom function’s purpose?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the ninja types /** in the editor, the closing comment symbol */ will automatically appear. The ninja can create a blank line between the symbols (the editor will automatically add * at the beginning of the line) to type out their comment. By using these symbols, this comment will appear whenever the cursor hovers over the name of the spawnFlame function.

💡 Previously, the ninja has always used // to begin a comment. This is useful for naming sections and organizing code in the editor. Using /** to contain a comment helps the coder to understand and remember the purpose of different custom functions in a project. This is especially helpful when a function is called in a different place than the function is defined; it provides an easy way to remember what the function’s code will do.

💡 Remind the ninja that just as when typing regular comments, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when adding comments to a function’s documentation box.
steps.instructions:
Use a comment to provide documentation for the function.


Add a blank line above the spawnFlame function definition, then type /** and notice how the MakeCode editor automatically ends the documentation comment with */. Add another blank line between the asterisks * and write a brief description of what the spawnFlame function will do.


By starting and ending the comment with a backslash / and starting each line with asterisks *, the comment will now be shown in the documentation box that appears whenever the cursor hovers over the spawnFlame function.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the function’s parameters in the setPosition and setScale code inside the curly brackets?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How are the function’s 3 parameters used in the setPosition and setScale code?

❓ Where will the Enemy sprite grow from when the spawnFlame function is called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the spawnFlame function is called, an Enemy sprite will be created with a flame as its image.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the function parameters can be used in the function’s definition code to customize the code. The parameter will be replaced by the argument passed in the function call.

💡 Remind the ninja that the setScale function assigns the sprite a scale based on the image’s dimension. The anchor determines which direction the sprite will expand or shrink. If the scale of a sprite’s image is increased from the middle, the sprite will grow equally from its center.
steps.instructions:
Set the Enemy sprite’s image, position, and initial scale inside the function definition!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { } of the spawnFlame function. Update the sprite name, then replace img`...` with the flame image variable and change the sprite kind to Enemy. 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x (x) y (y)] inside the curly brackets of the function definition. Replace mySprite with the Enemy sprite’s name, then use the function’s x and y parameters as the x and y positions.


Open Sprites again and drag [set (mySprite) scale to (1) anchor (ScaleAnchor.Middle)] underneath the existing code. Replace mySprite with the Enemy sprite’s name, then change the value parameter from 1 to the function parameter scale. Use the default anchor property ScaleAnchor.Middle, so that the Player sprite grows from its center.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you call the spawnFlame function inside the onUpdateInterval loop, passing the randX and randY variable arguments to the x and y parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the spawnFlame function is called inside of the onUpdateInterval loop? 

❓ How are the randX and randY variables used in the function call?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that a function needs to be defined then called separately, in order for its code to run. 

💡 When the onUpdateInterval loop is run, 2 random values will be selected and the spawnFlame function will be called. When the function is called, an Enemy sprite will be created and its x and y-positions will be set by the values selected by the 2 variables. The sprite’s scale will be set to 1. This will happen every 0.5 seconds in the project.
steps.instructions:
Call the spawnFlame function to place Enemy sprites on the screen!


Open Game and drag [run code on game update every (period) ms] underneath // game events. Inside the curly brackets of the onUpdateInterval loop, use the keyword let to declare 2 variables that will use randint to set the x and y-positions of the Enemy sprite so the sprites will appear anywhere across the lower part of the screen.


Call the spawnFlame function inside the onUpdateInterval loop. Under the 2 variable declarations, type the name of the function followed by a pair of parentheses. Inside the parentheses, pass arguments to the 3 parameters by typing the x-position variable, the y-position variable, and 1 to set the scale parameter. Separate each parameter with a comma. The code may look like: spawnFlame(randX, randY, 1)


Click ▶ to see flames appear at a regular interval, in random positions on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the vx and ay properties for the Enemy sprites inside the function definition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why do both the Enemy sprite’s x velocity and y acceleration need to be set?

❓ How is using the setFlag function to code a sprite to bounce on walls different than using the setBounceOnWall function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain the physics of the code to the ninja. In the spawnFlame function definition, the Enemy sprites are assigned a random x velocity from a range of positive and negative values. This means that the Enemy sprite will move either left or right on its own. The y acceleration of the Enemy sprite is set to simulate gravity for the Enemy sprite. This causes the sprite to fall and move in different directions on screen. The BounceOnWall sprite flag is used so that the Enemy sprite stays in screen and bounces to various positions.

💡 Previously in JavaScript, the ninja has used the setBounceOnWall function to code a sprite to bounce on walls. They can also use the setFlag function, which offers a list of many different sprite flags, to code a sprite to bounce on walls. This function uses the BounceOnWall function as a parameter.
steps.instructions:
Use physics to make the Enemy sprites bounce around the screen!


Inside the curly brackets of the spawnFlame function definition, set the Enemy sprite’s x velocity (vx) by typing the Enemy sprite name, a dot operator ., the vx property, and an assignment operator =. Use randint to assign each Enemy sprite a random vx value from -40 to 40.


Then, set the Enemy sprite’s y acceleration (ay) by typing the Enemy sprite name, a dot operator, the ay property, and an assignment operator =. Assign the value of ay to 50 so the Enemy sprites will bounce on their own.


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) (SpriteFlag.AutoDestroy) (on)] underneath the code. Update the sprite name, then change the flag parameter to BounceOnWall and the on parameter to true, so that the Enemy sprites bounce on walls. 


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprites move on their own and bounce around the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a fireInterval variable then update its value inside the onUpdateInterval loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How often will the spawnFlame function be called and new Enemy sprites created in the onUpdateInterval loop?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The spawnFlame function will be called and new Enemy sprites are created at the interval selected by the fireInterval variable. After the first loop runs, the fireInterval variable will be reassigned a random value in milliseconds. Each subsequent time the loop runs, a new value will be assigned to the variable.
steps.instructions:
Change the interval at which the Enemy sprites appear!


Underneath // game events, use the keyword let to declare a fireInterval variable to change the interval of the onUpdateInterval loop. Assign the variable a positive value in milliseconds, such as 3000.


Inside the parentheses of the onUpdateInterval loop, replace 500 with the fireInterval variable. 


Inside the curly brackets of the onUpdateInterval loop, under the spawnFlame function call, reassign fireInterval a random positive value, in milliseconds, using randint. 


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprites appear on screen at random intervals!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use setFlag to update the StayInScreen property so that the Player sprite doesn’t move off screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is using the setFlag function to set a sprite to stay in screen different than using the setStayInScreen function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Previously in JavaScript, the ninja has used the setStayInScreen function to prevent a sprite from moving off screen. They can also use the setFlag function, which offers a list of many different sprite flags, to code a sprite to stay in screen. This function uses the StayInScreen function as a parameter.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the project!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // game set up. Update the sprite name, then replace img`...` with the cloud image variable. 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x (x) y (y)] under the sprite creation code. Update the sprite name, then set the position to the top middle of the screen.


Allow the Player sprite to only move left and right across the screen. Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the existing code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name then add the vx and vy parameters so the Player sprite can only move left to right. 


Keep the Player sprite in screen. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) (SpriteFlag.AutoDestroy) (on)] underneath the existing code. Update the sprite name, then change the flag parameter to StayInScreen and the on parameter to true.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite move left and right across the top of the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use setScale on the Projectile sprite and change the value parameter to make the raindrop appear smaller on the screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the A button is pressed?

❓ What values might be used as arguments in the createProjectileFromSprite code so that a projectile is sent from the Player sprite and falls down towards the Enemy sprites?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the A button is pressed, a Projectile sprite will be sent from the Player sprite towards the Enemy sprite. The Projectile sprite’s scale will be set to 0.75 (25% smaller than its full size).

💡 Remind the ninja that the vx parameter of the createProjectileFromSprite code will set the speed at which the projectile moves horizontally on the screen and the vy parameter will set the speed at which the projectile moves vertically on the screen. The projectile should only move vertically in this project.
steps.instructions:
Send projectiles from the Player sprite to destroy the Enemy sprites!


Open Controller and drag [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath // game events. Use the default property A and default event Pressed.


Open Sprites and drag [projectile (img) from (mySprite) with vx (vx) vy (vy)] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event. Name the sprite rainDrop and use the rain image variable as the projectile’s image. Update the other 3 parameters so that the projectile will be sent from the Player sprite and move down the screen towards the Enemy sprites.


Open Sprites again and drag [set (mySprite) scale to (1) anchor (ScaleAnchor.Middle)] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event. Replace mySprite with the Projectile sprite’s name, then change the value parameter from 1 to 0.75 to make the raindrop appear smaller on screen. 


Click ▶ and press the A button to create raindrop projectiles from the Player sprite!

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the z-position to the correct depth so the Player sprite appears in front of the projectiles?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ In what order will the Player and Projectile sprites appear on the screen? How do you know?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Because the Player sprite is assigned a z-position of 2, it will appear in front of the Projectile sprites that are sent from it (which will be assigned a default z-position of 1).

💡 Point out to the ninja that adjusting the z property of sprites typically has to do with game design and supporting game play. When a user plays a game, it’s important that what they see is realistic and engaging. It would be confusing for the user if the raindrop appeared in front of the cloud, instead of behind it.
steps.instructions:
Set the depth level of the Player sprite so that the projectiles appear from behind it!


Below the Player sprite’s existing code, type the name of the Player sprite followed by a dot operator. Select the z property from the code completion tool then type an assignment operator. Set the z-position to 2 so the Player sprite appears in front of the Projectile sprites.


Click ▶ to see how the depth level changes the order in which sprites appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use sprite and otherSprite in the 2 destroy functions?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when a Projectile sprite and an Enemy sprite overlap? What else might happen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When a Projectile sprite and an Enemy sprite overlap, both sprites will be destroyed. In a later step, the ninja will add code to spawn 2 smaller Enemy sprites on overlap.
steps.instructions:
Destroy the Projectile and Enemy sprites when they overlap! 


Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath the controller.A event. Change the kind parameter to Projectile and otherKind parameter to Enemy. 


Open Sprites again and drag 2 [destroy (mySprite)] inside the curly brackets of the onOverlap event. Replace mySprite with sprite on one line, and with otherSprite on the other.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy and Projectile sprites disappear on overlap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you call the spawnFlame function twice inside an if conditional that checks whether the newScale variable is greater than 0.25?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when a Projectile sprite and an Enemy sprite overlap? 

❓ Where will the new Enemy sprites appear on screen? What size will they be?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When a Projectile sprite and an Enemy sprite overlap, both sprites will be destroyed and the newScale variable will store the new size of the Enemy sprite. The spawnFlame function will be called twice with arguments that will place the sprites at the same position of the previous Enemy sprite and will decrease their size by 25%.

💡 Point out to the ninja that similar to retrieving the x or y position of a sprite, the scale property of a sprite can also be retrieved by typing the sprite’s name and a dot operator. 

💡 Remind the ninja that variables can be used to pass an argument to a function’s parameter. This can be useful for using different values as a function’s parameter throughout a project.
steps.instructions:
Spawn 2 smaller Enemy sprites whenever a Projectile overlaps with an Enemy sprite!


Inside the curly brackets of the onOverlap event, use the keyword let to declare a newScale variable. Assign it to the value of the otherSprite scale using a dot operator and the scale property, then subtracting 0.25 


Open Logic and drag [if] underneath the newScale variable code. Check if the value of the newScale variable is greater than 0.25 inside the parentheses.


Inside the curly brackets of the if conditional, call the spawnFlame function by typing the name of the function followed by a pair of parentheses. Inside the parentheses, pass the otherSprite x and y-positions and the newScale variable to the function’s 3 parameters. The code may look like: 

spawnFlame(otherSprite.x, otherSprite.y, newScale)

Copy (Ctrl + C) and paste (Ctrl + V) the spawnFlame function call underneath the first function call to spawn a second smaller Enemy sprite.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprite spawn into 2 smaller sprites wherever it is overlapped by a Projectile sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use 2 if conditionals inside the onOverlap event to create win and lose conditions for the project by checking the length of the allOfKind array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the allOfKind function used to trigger the game to end? 

❓ When will the game end in a win or in a loss? What type of feedback might be shared with the user?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that the allOfKind function returns an array of all the sprites of the given kind. This function is used to check the length of the array of all Enemy sprites on screen to trigger the game to end.

💡 When there are 0 Enemy sprites on the screen, the game will end in a win. When there are 15 or more Enemy sprites on the screen, the game will end in a loss.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the setGameOverEffect function before the gameOver function to set an effect to play when the game over screen appears.
steps.instructions:
Add win or lose conditions to the project!


Open Logic and drag [if] underneath the existing code inside the curly brackets of the onOverlap event. 


Then, open Sprites and drag [array of sprites of kind (kind)] inside the parentheses of the conditional. Change the kind parameter to Enemy, then type a dot operator and length after the closing parenthesis. Use an equality operator to check if there are 0 Enemy sprites in the allOfKind array.


Open Game and drag [splash (title)] inside the curly brackets of the if conditional. Open Game again and drag [game over (true)] below the splash code. Update the parameters in the splash and game.gameOver code to end the game in a win.


Copy (Ctrl + C) and paste (Ctrl + V) the entire if conditional onto a new line inside the onOverlap event. Use a greater than or equal to relational operator to check if 15 or more Enemy sprites are in the allOfKind array. Update the parameters in the splash and game.gameOver code to end the game in a loss.


Click ▶ to test out the win and lose conditions.

steps.hints: ❓ What title or directions would help users understand how the game works?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What background image might you use as a backdrop for the project?

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a background image and sharing directions at the start of the project!


Open Scene and drag [start background image to (img)] above the Player sprite’s code under // game set up. Select a background image from the gallery or My Assets.


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] below the existing code underneath the setBackgroundImage code. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box shares directions for the user to follow.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses functions to spawn moving sprites.

validationItems.text: Create a spawnFlame function with 3 number parameters (x, y, and scale) to create moving enemy sprites.

requirements.match: function spawnFlame(x: number, y: number, scale: number)

validationItems.text: Use a comment to document the function.
Inside the spawnFlame function, set the Enemy sprite, its position, and initial scale.
Call the spawnFlame function in an onGameUpdateInterval loop to place Enemy sprites in random positions at an interval stored in a fireInterval variable.
Use physics to make the Enemy sprites bounce across the screen.
Add a Player sprite, set its position to the top middle of the screen, move it left and right with the controller, set it to stay in the screen, and set its depth.
Create projectiles from the player sprite when the A button is pressed.
Destroy the Projectile and Enemy sprites when they overlap and then spawn 2 smaller Enemy sprites using a newScale variable.
End the game in a win or a loss on Projectile/Enemy sprite overlap, depending on how many Enemy sprites are present on screen.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 5 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about functions. Functions can be used to name a unique chunk of code that can be easily reused in a project. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 5:

badges.title: Function Junction
badges.description: Create and call functions that use different parameter types in JavaScript.

badges.title: Functional Thinking
badges.description: Create a new function, with or without parameters, in JavaScript.

badges.title: Calling All Functions
badges.description: Call a function, with or without parameters, in JavaScript.

badges.title: Time for a Change
badges.description: Change the border color of the countdown timer.

badges.title: Feeling Shifty
badges.description: Use the shift function to remove and return the first value in an array.

badges.title: Read the Manual
badges.description: Use a block comment to document a function.
